The first time I noticed time behaving strangely was in an ordinary queue. It wasn’t dramatic—no clocks melting, no sudden silence—but the minutes kept arriving late to their own appointments. The people ahead of me shifted, glanced at their phones, sighed as if they were waiting for a train that should have already passed. I remember thinking that waiting has its own grammar: the way anticipation stacks, the way patience thins, the way hope makes room for disappointment.

When it finally moved, the line advanced by one person at a time, as though each step had to be negotiated. A laugh broke out somewhere near the front—soft, surprising—and then conversation loosened the air. I realized that time doesn’t just flow; it listens. It changes its pace depending on whether we’re clenching our hands or letting them rest. Later, I caught myself doing the same thing in my own life: rushing tasks so I could arrive “after,” and missing the small arrivals that were happening all along.

Now I try a different experiment. I choose one mundane moment—washing a mug, folding a shirt, walking to the mailbox—and give it my attention like a light turned on in a dark room. Not to slow everything down, exactly, but to see what was already there. In those moments, time feels less like a threat and more like a companion with a familiar, steady voice.
